{{Short description|Mathematical theorem in representation theory}}
'''Schur–Weyl duality''' is a mathematical theorem in [[representation theory]] that relates [[Irreducible representation|irreducible]] finite-dimensional [[Group representation|representations]] of the [[general linear group|general linear]] and [[symmetric group|symmetric]] groups. Schur–Weyl duality forms an archetypical situation in representation theory involving two kinds of [[symmetry]] that determine each other. It is named after two pioneers of representation theory of [[Lie group]]s, [[Issai Schur]], who discovered the phenomenon, and [[Hermann Weyl]], who popularized it in his books on [[quantum mechanics]] and [[classical groups]] as a way of classifying representations of [[unitary group|unitary]] and general linear groups.

Schur–Weyl duality can be proven using the [[double centralizer theorem]].<ref>{{citation|author1=Etingof, Pavel |author2=Golberg, Oleg |author3=Hensel, Sebastian |author4=Liu, Tiankai |author5=Schwendner, Alex |author6=Vaintrob, Dmitry |author7=Yudovina, Elena |title=Introduction to representation theory. With historical interludes by Slava Gerovitch|year=2011|zbl=1242.20001}}, Theorem 5.18.4</ref>

== Statement of the theorem ==
Consider the [[tensor]] space

: <math> \mathbb{C}^n\otimes\mathbb{C}^n\otimes\cdots\otimes\mathbb{C}^n </math> with ''k'' factors.

The [[symmetric group]] ''S''<sub>''k''</sub> on ''k'' letters [[Group action (mathematics)|acts]] on this space (on the left) by permuting the factors,

: <math> \sigma(v_1\otimes v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_k) = v_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}\otimes v_{\sigma^{-1}(2)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\sigma^{-1}(k)}.</math>

The general linear group ''GL''<sub>''n''</sub> of invertible ''n''&times;''n'' matrices acts on it by the simultaneous [[matrix multiplication]],

: <math> g(v_1\otimes v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_k) = gv_1\otimes gv_2\otimes\cdots\otimes gv_k, \quad g\in \text{GL}_n. </math>

These two actions [[Equivariant map|commute]], and in its concrete form, the Schur–Weyl duality asserts that under the joint action of the groups ''S''<sub>''k''</sub> and ''GL''<sub>''n''</sub>, the tensor space decomposes into a direct sum of tensor products of irreducible modules (for these two groups) that actually determine each other,

: <math> \mathbb{C}^n\otimes\mathbb{C}^n\otimes\cdots\otimes\mathbb{C}^n = \bigoplus_D \pi_k^D\otimes\rho_n^D. </math>

The summands are indexed by the [[Young diagram]]s ''D'' with ''k'' boxes and at most ''n'' rows, and representations <math>\pi_k^D</math> of ''S''<sub>''k''</sub> with different ''D'' are mutually non-isomorphic, and the same is true for representations <math>\rho_n^D</math> of ''GL''<sub>''n''</sub>.

The abstract form of the Schur–Weyl duality asserts that two algebras of operators on the tensor space generated by the actions of ''GL''<sub>''n''</sub> and ''S''<sub>''k''</sub> are the full mutual [[centralizer (ring theory)|centralizer]]s in the algebra of the endomorphisms <math>\mathrm{End}_\mathbb{C}(\mathbb{C}^n\otimes\mathbb{C}^n\otimes\cdots\otimes\mathbb{C}^n).</math>

== Example ==
Suppose that ''k'' = 2 and ''n'' is greater than one. Then the Schur–Weyl duality is the statement that the space of two-tensors decomposes into symmetric and antisymmetric  parts, each of which is an irreducible module for ''GL''<sub>''n''</sub>:

: <math> \mathbb{C}^n\otimes\mathbb{C}^n = S^2\mathbb{C}^n \oplus \Lambda^2\mathbb{C}^n.</math>

The symmetric group ''S''<sub>''2''</sub> consists of two elements and has two irreducible representations, the [[trivial representation]] and the [[sign representation]]. The trivial representation of ''S''<sub>2</sub> gives rise to the symmetric tensors, which are invariant (i.e. do not change) under the permutation of the factors, and the sign representation corresponds to the skew-symmetric tensors, which flip the sign.

== Proof ==
First consider the following setup:
*''G'' a [[finite group]],
*<math>A = \mathbb{C}[G]</math> the [[Group ring|group algebra]] of ''G'',
*<math>U</math> a finite-dimensional [[Module_(mathematics)|right ''A''-module]], and
*<math>B = \operatorname{End}_G(U)</math>, which acts on ''U'' from the left and commutes with the right action of ''G'' (or of ''A''). In other words, <math>B</math> is the centralizer of <math>A</math> in the endomorphism ring <math>\operatorname{End}_\C(U)</math>.

The proof uses two algebraic lemmas.

{{math_theorem|name=Lemma 1|math_statement=<ref>{{harvnb|Fulton|Harris|1991|loc=Lemma 6.22.}}</ref> If <math>W</math> is a simple left ''A''-module, then <math>U \otimes_A W</math> is a simple left ''B''-module.
}}

''Proof'': Since ''U'' is [[semisimple representation|semisimple]] by [[Maschke's theorem]], there is a decomposition <math>U = \bigoplus_i U_i^{\oplus m_i}</math> into simple ''A''-modules. Then <math>U \otimes_A W = \bigoplus_i (U_i \otimes_A W)^{\oplus m_i}</math>. Since ''A'' is the left [[regular representation]] of ''G'', each simple ''G''-module appears in ''A'' and we have that <math>U_i \otimes_A W = \mathbb{C}</math> (respectively zero) if and only if <math>U_i, W</math> correspond to the same simple factor of ''A'' (respectively otherwise). Hence, we have: <math>U \otimes_A W = (U_{i_0} \otimes_A W)^{\oplus m_{i_0}} = \mathbb{C}^{\oplus m_{i_0}}.</math> Each nonzero vector in <math>\mathbb{C}^{\oplus m_{i_0}}</math> generates the whole space as a ''B''-module and so <math>U \otimes_A W</math> is simple. (In general, a nonzero module is simple if and only if each of its nonzero cyclic submodule coincides with the module.) <math>\square</math>

{{math_theorem|name=Lemma 2|math_statement=<ref>{{harvnb|Fulton|Harris|1991|loc=Lemma 6.23.}}</ref> When <math>U = V^{\otimes d}</math> and ''G'' is the symmetric group <math>\mathfrak{S}_d</math>, a subspace of <math>U</math> is a ''B''-submodule if and only if it is invariant under <math>\operatorname{GL}(V)</math>; in other words, a ''B''-submodule is the same as a <math>\operatorname{GL}(V)</math>-submodule.
}}

''Proof'': Let <math>W = \operatorname{End}(V)</math>. Then <math>W \hookrightarrow \operatorname{End}(U), w \mapsto w^d = d! w \otimes \cdots \otimes w</math>. Also, the image of ''W'' spans the subspace of symmetric tensors <math>\operatorname{Sym}^d(W)</math>. Since <math>B = \operatorname{Sym}^d(W)</math>, the image of <math>W</math> spans <math>B</math>. Since <math>\operatorname{GL}(V)</math> is dense in ''W'' either in the Euclidean topology or in the [[Zariski topology]], the assertion follows. <math>\square</math>

The Schur–Weyl duality now follows. We take <math>G = \mathfrak{S}_d</math> to be the symmetric group and <math>U = V^{\otimes d}</math> the ''d''-th tensor power of a finite-dimensional complex [[vector space]] ''V''.

Let <math>V^{\lambda}</math> denote the irreducible <math>\mathfrak{S}_d</math>-representation corresponding to a partition <math>\lambda</math> and <math>m_{\lambda} = \dim V^{\lambda}</math>. Then by Lemma 1
:<math>S^{\lambda}(V) := V^{\otimes d} \otimes_{\mathfrak{S}_d} V^{\lambda}</math>
is irreducible as a <math>\operatorname{GL}(V)</math>-module. Moreover, when <math>A = \bigoplus_{\lambda} (V^{\lambda})^{\oplus m_\lambda}</math> is the left semisimple decomposition, we have:<ref>{{harvnb|Fulton|Harris|1991|loc=Theorem 6.3. (2), (4)}}</ref>
:<math>V^{\otimes d} = V^{\otimes d} \otimes_A A = \bigoplus_{\lambda} (V^{\otimes d} \otimes_{\mathfrak{S}_d} V^{\lambda})^{\oplus m_{\lambda}}</math>,
which is the semisimple decomposition as a <math>\operatorname{GL}(V)</math>-module.

== Generalizations ==

The [[Brauer algebra]] plays the role of the symmetric group in the generalization of the Schur-Weyl duality to the orthogonal and symplectic groups. The generalization to mixed-tensorial representations of general linear groups involves the [[Walled-Brauer algebra]].

More generally, the [[partition algebra]] and its subalgebras give rise to a number of generalizations of the Schur-Weyl duality.
